title: More in imagination
hook: we suffer more in imagination than in reality

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pacuvius. Your line was a whole life. Did you lie down last night and say, I have lived? Day four hundred forty-eight. The end of a week.

Your boss sends a message at four forty-five on a Friday: can we talk Monday? That's all. No subject. And by Saturday morning you've lived through the whole meeting a dozen times. You've been criticized, demoted, let go. You've drafted your defense. Then on Monday it turns out she wanted to ask which conference room you like. Two days of suffering for something that never happened. Seneca's thirteenth letter catches this habit in a single sentence. Today: more in imagination.
screen: `CAN WE TALK MONDAY?` → `A WHOLE WEEKEND OF DREAD.` → `MORE IN IMAGINATION.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Seneca tells Lucilius that more things frighten us than actually hurt us. And then, in Gummere's translation: we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. Second, the three mistakes. Some things, Seneca says, torment us more than they should. Some torment us before they should. And some torment us when they shouldn't at all. We exaggerate a trouble, we imagine one that isn't there, or we start suffering it early. Third, the test. So he gives a simple test. When a fear arrives, look at it closely. Is this trouble here now, or still in the future? If it's coming, is it certain, or only likely? And is it really an evil, or does it just feel like one? Much of what we dread, he says, never arrives. Between now and then, a lot can change. Fourth, the week. Look at what Seneca has handed us these seven days: one is enough. All mine is with me. As if seen. Cato. We grew old together. A whole life. And now, more in the mind. One thread runs through them: much of what weighs on us lives in our heads, not in the world, and the world is often kinder than our forecasts. That's not a promise that nothing bad will happen. Seneca had real troubles, and some arrived. It's a habit: check the fear against the facts before you suffer it in full. Often the meeting is about conference rooms.
screen: `MORE FRIGHTENS US THAN HURTS US.` · `TOO MUCH, TOO SOON, OR FOR NOTHING.` · `HERE NOW? CERTAIN? REALLY BAD?` · `THE WEEK: CHECK THE FORECAST.` · then, large: `MORE IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're worried about. Let it come in clearly. Now ask Seneca's questions, slowly, one at a time. Is it happening right now, or later? If later, is it certain, or only possible? If it does happen, how bad would it really be, and what could I do? Notice how much of the worry was in the forecast. Then come back to this moment: your breath, your chair, nothing happening yet. The bell holds the time.
Opinione. Seneca's thirteenth letter, in Latin: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, so check each fear against the facts. Today's word.
Your line: more in the mind. The next time a worry grows today, ask: here now, certain, really bad? Check it against what you actually know. Day four hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism question a fear before acting on it: is it present, is it certain, and is it truly bad?

original.note: Latin: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, from Seneca's thirteenth letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't worry, be happy.
what it means: Seneca says we suffer more in imagination than in reality, and gives a test: is it present, certain, truly bad?
what a scholar hears: the Latin says opinione, by opinion, the same Stoic idea as Epictetus: it's our judgments about things that trouble us.
